headline: Wholesale prices were flat in July and their annual rate fell to 4.7% from 5.5%, the odds of a September rate rise dropped to about a third, and the S&P 500 closed at a record — with retail sales due at 8:30 this morning.
stance: The second inflation report of the week was as harmless as the first. Producer prices — what companies charge each other, one step before the shelf — were unchanged in July, and the annual rate fell to 4.7% from 5.5% in June, helped by energy prices falling 3.1% on the month and gasoline 5.7%. Rate futures took another step: the chance the Fed leaves its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in September rose to roughly 66%, from 62% a day earlier, putting a quarter-point rise at about 34%. Stocks used it — the S&P 500 rose 0.65% to 7,798.99, a record close, the Nasdaq 100 0.81% to 26,803.03 and the Dow 0.13% to 53,839.99. Bonds did the more interesting thing: the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.63% from 4.68% and the 2-year to 4.15% from 4.20%, while the annual inflation rate bond prices imply eased to 2.24% from 2.26% — a repricing of policy, again, rather than of inflation. One caveat sits inside the report: the measure that strips out food, energy and trade margins rose 0.4% on the month, the firm part of an otherwise soft print. The last data of the week — July retail sales at 8:30am ET and consumer sentiment at 10:00 — is the read on whether the household side is holding up.

news.head: Wholesale prices were flat in July
news.body: The government's producer-price report, released Thursday at 8:30am ET, showed prices charged by US producers unchanged on the month, with the annual rate falling to 4.7% from 5.5% in June. Goods prices fell 0.7% while services rose 0.2%; energy fell 3.1% and gasoline 5.7%. Goods excluding food and energy rose 0.1%. The firmer part: the measure that excludes food, energy and trade margins rose 0.4% on the month and 4.7% over the year.

news.head: September moved again, in the same direction
news.body: After the report, rate-futures pricing put the chance the Fed holds its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in September at roughly 66%, up from 62% a day earlier, and the implied odds of a quarter-point rise at about 34%, down from 38%. Two benign inflation reports in two days have taken the September question from a coin flip at the start of the week to a clear lean toward no change. The minutes of the July meeting are published on August 19.

news.head: Jobless claims rose but the trend did not
news.body: Initial claims for unemployment benefits were 209,000 in the week ended August 8, up 9,000 from the prior week's revised 200,000. The four-week average, which smooths the weekly noise, was unchanged at 199,000. Continuing claims — people still drawing benefits — fell 22,000 to 1,777,000 in the week ended August 1, with the insured unemployment rate at 1.2%.

news.head: A record close, and two of the week's best results were sold
news.body: The S&P 500 finished at a record on Thursday. Underneath it, Cisco fell 8.4% the day after reporting revenue up 18% and $9.3 billion of AI orders for the fiscal year — a beat that ran into what was already expected of it. Applied Materials then reported after the close and was down about 5% before Friday's open on its own record quarter.

news.head: Applied Materials had its best quarter and its shares fell anyway
news.body: The chip-equipment maker reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $9.115 billion, up 25% on a year earlier, with adjusted earnings of $3.50 a share, up 41%, and $3.17 on the stricter accounting measure. Semiconductor systems contributed $7.040 billion and services $1.781 billion. It guided the current quarter to $10.25 billion of revenue, give or take $500 million, and $4.02 a share, give or take 20 cents. Revenue from memory chips used in AI servers rose 52% on a year earlier. The shares were down about 5% in trading before Friday's open.

news.head: Both oil forecasters cut their demand numbers on the same day
news.body: The International Energy Agency now expects global oil demand to fall by 1.6 million barrels a day in 2026, a downgrade of about 510,000 barrels a day from its July forecast. OPEC still expects growth, but cut it to roughly 600,000 barrels a day from 780,000. Brent settled at $86.96 on Thursday from $88.37 Wednesday and US crude at $81.21 from $82.58. US crude stockpiles rose 17.4 million barrels in the prior week.

news.head: Overnight: Korea led, Hong Kong lagged, US futures little changed
news.body: In trading through early Friday, the Kospi in Seoul rose 2.4%, Japan's Nikkei 225 0.6% and Germany's DAX 0.5%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.1%, Australia's benchmark 0.8% and the FTSE 100 in London 0.3%. S&P 500 futures were up 0.1% and Dow futures down 0.1% around 5:30am ET. Brent was about 1% higher overnight near $87.96 and the yen firmer at ¥159.16 to the dollar.

implications: Two soft inflation prints in one week have changed the lean, not the decision. A September hold at roughly 66% means the market now treats no change as the base case rather than a coin flip — but the thing that started this move was last week's 23,000 contraction in July payrolls, not the price data. The inflation reports removed an obstacle; they did not supply the reason.

The bond market repriced policy, not inflation. The 10-year yield fell 5 basis points to 4.63% and the 2-year 5 basis points to 4.15%, leaving the gap between them unchanged at 48 basis points. The annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next decade eased only to 2.24% from 2.26%, so the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield — down to 2.39% from 2.42% — did nearly all the work. Expected swings in Treasury prices fell for a second straight session, to 69.2 from 72.1.

Good results being sold is the more useful signal this week. Cisco fell 8.4% on a beat-and-raise and Applied Materials was down about 5% before Friday's open on record revenue growing 25%. When two AI-adjacent companies deliver and both trade lower, the constraint is what was already in the price, not what the businesses did — into a market whose cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio sits at 42.65, up from 42.3 a day earlier.

The cash cushion in the banking system is draining, quietly. The Treasury's own cash account rose to $964.0 billion in Wednesday's weekly snapshot from $907.3 billion a week earlier, and bank reserves fell to $2,944.1 billion from $2,993.3 billion — the Treasury rebuilding its balance pulls cash out of the banks. The Fed's overnight parking facility, which used to absorb the swings, held $0.5 billion Thursday against $0.7 billion Wednesday. Short-term funding spreads show no strain at all yet, which is why this is a watch item rather than a worry.

watch.head: July retail sales, 8:30am ET
watch.body: Estimates for the headline month-on-month figure run from flat to +0.3%. The measure excluding cars is seen at +0.2% after a 0.2% fall in June, and the control group that feeds directly into GDP at +0.4%. With gasoline prices down in July, the ex-gasoline detail matters more than the top line.

watch.head: Consumer sentiment, 10:00am ET
watch.body: The preliminary August reading of the University of Michigan survey is expected at 54.4 against 55.2 in July. The part worth reading is the inflation expectations inside it: 4.2% for the year ahead and 3.3% for the next five years in the prior survey. Two soft producer and consumer price reports mean little if households still expect 4%.

watch.head: Whether the market keeps selling good news
watch.body: Applied Materials was down about 5% before Friday's open after record results, a day after Cisco fell 8.4% on a beat. How that opens today is the cleanest read available on whether the AI trade is discounting execution rather than rewarding it — and the chip-equipment names are the machinery layer beneath everything Cisco described on Wednesday.

watch.head: Weekly futures positioning, this afternoon
watch.body: The regulator's weekly report on what speculators are actually holding lands this afternoon. Last week's showed three new extremes in one go: speculators flipping to almost no bullish bets in 10-year Treasuries and in Nasdaq 100 futures, and to heavily positioned long in the dollar. Whether those held through a week of falling yields and a record equity close is the question this afternoon answers.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since yesterday morning: the producer-price report came and went as harmlessly as the consumer one. Prices charged by US producers were unchanged on the month and the annual rate fell to 4.7% from 5.5% in June. Goods fell 0.7% and services rose 0.2%; energy fell 3.1% and gasoline 5.7%. The one firm spot is the measure that strips out food, energy and trade margins, up 0.4% on the month and 4.7% over the year — the soft headline is an energy story, not a broad one.

Rate futures moved with it: a September hold now prices at roughly 66%, from 62% a day earlier, and a quarter-point rise at about 34%, from 38%. The July meeting minutes are published on August 19, and there is one more consumer-price report before the September 15-16 decision.

The labour check came in the same hour. Initial claims for unemployment benefits were 209,000 in the week ended August 8, up 9,000 on a revised 200,000, while the four-week average held at 199,000. Continuing claims fell 22,000 to 1,777,000 in the week ended August 1, with 1.2% of the insured workforce drawing benefits. A single weekly rise on an unchanged average is noise, not a turn.

Treasuries rallied on it: the 10-year yield closed Thursday at 4.63% from 4.68% Wednesday and the 2-year at 4.15% from 4.20%, leaving the gap between them unchanged at +48 basis points. The 10-year breakeven — the annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next decade — eased to 2.24% from 2.26% and the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield to 2.39% from 2.42%. Expected swings in Treasury prices fell for a second straight session, to 69.2 from 72.1.

Elsewhere in the prior close: gold fell to $4,407.10 from $4,469 and silver to $64.59 from $65.53, while Brent settled at $86.96 from $88.37 and US crude at $81.21 from $82.58 after both major oil forecasters cut their demand numbers. The dollar index was 99.95 from 99.99, the yen ¥159.46 from ¥159.39, the euro $1.1533. Corn fell back to 472.25 cents a bushel from 481, easing to the 87th percentile of its three-year range.

Overnight into Friday: the Kospi rose 2.4%, the Nikkei 225 0.6% and the DAX 0.5%, while the Hang Seng fell 1.1% and the FTSE 100 0.3%. S&P 500 futures were up 0.1% around 5:30am ET. July retail sales arrive at 8:30am ET and consumer sentiment at 10:00.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: speculators moved to an extended short position in 10-year Treasury futures — the 12th percentile of the past three years, down 17 percentile points in a single week. Read straight, that is a contrarian-bullish lean for bonds: the crowd is set up for yields to rise, and the yield instead fell 5 basis points on Thursday to 4.63%. When positioning is that one-sided, a move against it tends to feed on itself.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Thursday's close: the S&P 500 rose 0.65% to 7,798.99, a record close, the Nasdaq 100 0.81% to 26,803.03 and the Dow 0.13% to 53,839.99. That is a second straight session of gains, and this time the index-level move was broader than the leadership underneath it.

Cisco fell 8.4% on Thursday, the day after reporting revenue up 18% on a year earlier and $9.3 billion of AI orders for the fiscal year. Nothing in the results deteriorated between Wednesday night and Thursday's close — what changed is that the bar had already been raised into the print.

Applied Materials reported after Thursday's close: fiscal third-quarter revenue of $9.115 billion, up 25%, adjusted earnings of $3.50 a share, up 41%, and $3.17 on the stricter accounting measure. Semiconductor systems contributed $7.040 billion and services $1.781 billion, with revenue from the memory chips used in AI servers up 52% on a year earlier. It guided the current quarter to $10.25 billion give or take $500 million, and $4.02 a share give or take 20 cents. The shares were down about 5% before Friday's open, having more than doubled so far in 2026.

Protection got slightly more expensive even as the index set a record: the VIX closed at 14.63 from 14.55 Wednesday and its Nasdaq-100 counterpart at 21.23 from 20.97. The skew index, which measures what investors pay for insurance against a large drop specifically, fell to 134.4 from 136.5 — ordinary hedges bid, tail hedges offered, the mirror image of Wednesday.

Breadth kept improving on the fast measure: 71.1% of S&P 500 members closed above their 50-day trend line, from 66.5% Wednesday, and 68% of Nasdaq-100 members, from 63%. On the slower 200-day measure it was 72.8% and 72% — the second of those unchanged. Participation is broadening over days, and only slowly over months.
Valuation kept pace with the price: the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which averages a decade of inflation-adjusted profits, sits at 42.65 from 42.3 a day earlier.
sections.positioning: The standing setup here has not changed, but the tape has moved against it. Speculators' bullish bets in Nasdaq 100 futures sit at the 1st percentile of the past three years, with hedgers at the opposite extreme — an extended short built the week before the index rose in each of the last two sessions and the S&P set a record. Two higher closes against that position is the part that is new; the position itself was in place beforehand and is not a warning that the market will fall.

single_name.note: (Portillo's, the fast-casual restaurant chain) — new to the screen in Thursday's scan, its first session on the list. An insider purchase was filed on Wednesday, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and both the scan's dark-pool and options signals are live. Nothing else on the current list is this fresh — every other name has been there at least two sessions.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit did nothing again, which given the week's news is itself the point: the extra yield high-yield bonds pay over investment-grade was 271 basis points in Wednesday's reading from 272 on Tuesday, with investment-grade spreads unchanged at 79. Two inflation reports, an oil-demand downgrade and a record equity close moved this not at all.

The cash cushion drained. The Treasury's own account at the Fed rose to $964.0 billion in Wednesday's weekly snapshot from $907.3 billion a week earlier, and bank reserves fell to $2,944.1 billion from $2,993.3 billion — when the Treasury rebuilds its balance, the cash comes out of the banking system. The Fed's overnight parking facility, which used to absorb exactly this, held $0.5 billion Thursday against $0.7 billion Wednesday. It has no absorbing left to do.

Despite that, the plumbing is quiet: the key bank-funding spreads sat at minus 1 basis point and the commercial-paper funding spread at 21 basis points in the latest readings. A $49 billion drop in reserves with no move in funding costs says the system still has more cash than it needs.

Broad financial conditions remain easier than average on both national measures — one at -0.58 and the other at -0.77 in the readings for the week to August 7, where negative means looser than normal. The Fed's balance sheet is 1.75% larger than a year ago, the yield on newly syndicated loans is 7.08%, and stocks and credit continue to move together more than usual, with the correlation between them at 0.68.
sections.positioning: No positioning extreme is flagged anywhere in the credit book for a third week — the only one of the five markets tracked with nothing stretched in it, while rates, equities, currencies and commodities each carry at least one three-year extreme. The thing to track in credit right now is not positioning but the reserve drain above: spreads are the last place strain shows up, and the funding market is the first.
